The Atlantic bumper (Chloroscombrus chrysurus) attains a maximum recorded total length of 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters] in the wild, representing the largest individuals documented across the species' western Atlantic range. Field surveys along the Brazilian coast indicate that females first achieve sexual maturation at a relatively modest size, with the total length at puberty measured at 12.4 centimeters [Lp = 12.4 centimeters], a value consistent with the early maturation strategy observed in many carangid fishes inhabiting warm, productive shelf waters. This moderate length at the onset of reproductive capability is coupled with a wet weight at puberty of approximately 20.2 grams [Wwp = approximately 20.2 grams], a body mass that reflects the considerable somatic growth still ahead before asymptotic size is approached. The ultimate wet weight for the species has been estimated at 2630 grams [Wwi = 2630 grams], a maximum adult mass derived from length-weight regressions applied to the length of 65 centimeters. This nearly two-order-of-magnitude increase in mass between puberty and adulthood highlights the protracted growth trajectory and the substantial energetic reserves required to sustain the species' pelagic, actively swimming lifestyle in subtropical and tropical coastal ecosystems.

This brief embryonic phase is typical of warm-water marine teleosts and reflects the elevated metabolic rates and accelerated developmental kinetics driven by the thermal regime. Newly hatched individuals are minute; the dry weight at birth is a mere 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a value consistent with the egg diameter of roughly 1 millimeter that characterizes the species' pelagic spawning strategy. The yolk-sac larva then enters a non-feeding, lecithotrophic stage during which the yolk is progressively resorbed, providing the sole source of nourishment until the mouth opens and the larva commences first exogenous feeding, a critical trophic transition.

The maximum reproductive output of Atlantic bumper has been quantified through field-based assessments of batch fecundity and spawning frequency. Gravid females produce a maximum annual reproductive output of approximately 106,200 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 106,200 eggs per year], a prodigious fecundity that compensates for the high rates of egg and larval mortality typical of pelagic spawners in the coastal environment. This corresponds to daily spawning events during the peak season, with each event yielding several hundred oocytes, but the key measure for this species remains the total annual egg production rather than per-event counts. All spawning and reproductive measurements were obtained from fish captured and maintained at a stable water temperature of 26.2 °C [T = 26.2 °C], which represents the thermal optimum for gonadal recrudescence and oocyte maturation in this species. Spawning occurs primarily during the late spring and summer months in the northern portion of the range.

The lifespan of Chloroscombrus chrysurus has been estimated from length-frequency analysis and otolith-based age determination conducted on individuals from the Gulf of Mexico and southeastern United States. Maximum recorded longevity under natural conditions is approximately 3650 days [am = approximately 3650 days], equivalent to roughly 10 years, for fish inhabiting waters with a mean annual temperature near 26.2 °C [T = 26.2 °C]. This decadal lifespan is modest relative to some larger, slower-growing carangids but is consistent with the relatively fast life history of this moderately sized, schooling pelagic species. The oldest individuals, which approach the asymptotic length of 65 centimeters, exhibit slower annual growth increments in their later years, indicative of a growth pattern that decelerates markedly after the onset of reproductive maturity. The age-based demographic data align well with the species' observed high natural mortality rates early in life followed by a period of lower, relatively constant adult mortality.

In addition to its life history traits, the Atlantic bumper exhibits notable physiological and ecological characteristics that shape its role in coastal food webs. The species is an active, visual predator that feeds predominantly on zooplankton, small crustaceans, and larval fish, employing a ram-feeding strategy in open water. Comparative studies within the Carangidae suggest that the combination of a 65 centimeter [Li = 65 centimeter] ultimate total length and a 2630 gram [Wwi = 2630 gram] ultimate wet weight places Chloroscombrus chrysurus among the medium-sized members of the family, with a body shape optimized for sustained swimming and brief bursts of speed. The extraordinarily high fecundity, estimated at 106,200 eggs per year [Ri = 106,200 eggs per year], reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes numerical output over parental investment, a common adaptation among pelagic marine spawners facing intense egg and larval predation. This iteroparous reproductive pattern, combined with the rapid early growth from a 0.00052 gram [Wwb = 0.00052 gram] larval stage to a 20.2 gram [Wwp = 20.2 gram] pubertal mass, underscores the species' capacity to exploit productive coastal environments through a combination of high reproductive effort and efficient energy conversion.
